title: John the Baptist: locusts or honey cake?
subtitle: Matthew and Mark say locusts; the Jewish-Christian gospel Epiphanius quoted says honey that tasted of manna. Both readings, the texts behind each, the debate moments where it came up, and what is still open.

it: 1 · WHAT WAS SAID IN THE DEBATE
3 · THE CASE FOR THE HONEY CAKE

THE QUESTION

What did John the Baptist eat in the wilderness?

Matthew 3:4 and Mark 1:6 say "locusts and wild honey". A Jewish-Christian gospel that Epiphanius quoted around 375 says wild honey "which tasted of manna, like a cake made with oil", and no locusts. In Greek the two words are one letter apart: AKRIS, locust, and ENKRIS, cake.

It came up in the debate on POST Post-Modern Theology (October 2026) between Kam Waters and Aaron Abke and Dallas and Post, from 3:07:34. This board puts both readings on the table with the texts behind them.

WHAT WAS SAID

The exchange runs about eight minutes inside a longer argument over whether Epiphanius was reading the Hebrew gospel in Greek.

ONE SIDE: Epiphanius read Greek, saw a one-letter change, and said so. The gospels say locusts.

THE OTHER (Kam): the pun cuts both ways, so look at the larger body of evidence: carob, a honey-cake tradition in the fathers, manna, and a passage in Kings.

The checks beside each moment say what the held texts show.
Then what about the the locust and the honeycomb?
making cakes something in Greek into locust something in Greek

CHECK · HOLDS

Panarion 30,13,5 is the passage. In Craig Wescoe's translation: "so that, no doubt, they may turn the word of truth into a lie and make it a cake in honey instead of locusts." The Greek, checked against Holl's edition in the October audit, has ἐγκρίς (cake) "instead of" ἀκρίδων (locusts).

(christianity/Incoming/epiphanius-panarion-book-1-full-text.md, 30,13,5; audits/2026-10-20-panarion-quotations.md, row 38)
So, when you when you look at the pun, it can cut both ways.

CHECK · HOLDS, BOTH WAYS

A pun that only works in Greek tells you the difference arose in Greek. It does not tell you which word came first. Both sides agree Epiphanius held a Greek copy; the argument is about direction.
we definitely know it wasn't locust bugs

CHECK · NARROWER THAN SAID

"We definitely know it wasn't locust bugs" is more than the held texts show.

MANNA: holds. Brenton's Septuagint gives the manna "the taste of it as a wafer with honey" (Exodus 16:31) and "as the taste [of] wafer made with oil" (Numbers 11:8), the same two descriptions the Ebionite verse combines.

KINGS: holds, in the Greek Bible. 3 Kingdoms 12:24i (Brenton): "bread, and two cakes, and grapes, and a pot of honey". KJV 1 Kings 14:3 has loaves, cracknels and a cruse of honey.

A HONEY-CAKE TRADITION IN THE FATHERS: not in what we hold. Justin and Jerome both say locusts; Epiphanius reports the honey cake only to condemn it.

CAROB: see section 4. No held ancient text says it.
The Gospels say that John ate locusts
I believe the Greek is earlier than the Hebrew

CHECK · HOLDS

Matthew 3:4 and Mark 1:6 say locusts, in the KJV and in the held Westcott-Hort Greek (ακριδες, ακριδας). The answer at 3:14:36, that the Greek is earlier than the Hebrew, is where the real disagreement lies: which text is older.

THE CASE FOR LOCUSTS

It is the reading of every gospel text we hold, it was lawful food, the wilderness community of the scrolls legislated how to eat it, and the fathers we hold who mention John's food read it.

The strongest single point: Mark, the gospel most scholars date earliest, says locusts, and the Ebionite reading survives only in a hostile quotation from the fourth century.

THE GREEK

Matthew 3:4 (Westcott-Hort): "η δε τροφη ην αυτου ακριδες και μελι αγριον", his food was locusts and wild honey.

Mark 1:6: "και εσθων ακριδας και μελι αγριον", and eating locusts and wild honey.

(christianity/Incoming/greek-nt-westcott-hort/01-matthew.md, 02-mark.md)

We know of no Greek manuscript of either gospel that reads cake here. Confirming that properly needs a critical apparatus, which the library does not hold yet.

LAWFUL FOOD

Leviticus 11:22 names four kinds of locust as clean, the one class of insect the Law allows. A Torah-keeping Jew in the wilderness could eat them.

THE SCROLLS COMMUNITY ATE THEM

The Damascus Document, the rule of the same movement as the Dead Sea Scrolls, sets out how locusts are to be killed, and in the same passage how fish are to be bled. This is the strongest point against an Essene-style vegetarian John, and our own boards have flagged it before.

Not held: the page beside this is outside the library and names no translator. A named translation is on the list in section 6.
Damascus Document XII 11-15, "Of food" (translator not named on the page)
As for the various kinds of locust, these are to be put in fire or water while they are still alive

THE FATHERS WE HOLD SAY LOCUSTS

Justin Martyr, about 155: John was "eating nothing but locusts and wild honey" (Dialogue with Trypho 88; christianity/Incoming/justin-martyr-dialogue-with-trypho-full-text.md).

Jerome, around 400: John "had for his meat locusts and wild honey" (Letter 107, to Laeta), and "his diet of locusts and wild honey" was designed "to encourage virtue and continence" (Letter 125, to Rusticus; christianity/Incoming/jerome-letters-full-text.md).

A TWIST: EVEN EPIPHANIUS DID NOT COUNT LOCUSTS AS MEAT

Panarion 30,19,3: "'not eating nor drinking' means that John took no share of meat or wine, but partook only of locusts and honey — and plainly of water too."

(christianity/Incoming/epiphanius-panarion-book-1-full-text.md, 30,19,3)

So the man who defends the locusts against the Ebionites also says John ate no meat. On his reading, locusts and a fleshless John are not in conflict. That matters for how much the locusts are made to carry, on either side.

THE CASE FOR THE HONEY CAKE

The gospel Epiphanius says the Ebionites used, a Jewish-Christian movement, had John living on wild honey that tasted of manna: the bread from heaven Israel ate in the wilderness. The texts around John's food point the same way: a Nazirite from the womb, "neither eating bread nor drinking wine". And Jewish-Christian tradition remembered James, the brother of Jesus, as eating no flesh.

Its weakness is that we have the verse only from its enemy, in one quotation, with no manuscript of the gospel itself.

THE VERSE ITSELF

Panarion 30,13,4b-c (trans. Craig Wescoe): "And John had clothing made from camel's hair, and a belt of leather round his loins. And his food, it says, was wild honey, which tasted of manna, like a cake made with oil".

30,13,5: "so that, no doubt, they may turn the word of truth into a lie and make it a cake in honey instead of locusts."

(christianity/Incoming/epiphanius-panarion-book-1-full-text.md)

NOT A RANDOM PUN: IT IS THE MANNA WORD

The Septuagint, the Greek Bible, describes manna with this word. Brenton's translation renders it "wafer" both times:

Exodus 16:31: "the taste of it as a wafer with honey."
Numbers 11:8: "the sweetness of it was as the taste [of] wafer made with oil."

(christianity/Incoming/septuagint-brenton/02-exodus.md, 04-numbers.md)

The Ebionite verse joins the two: honey, manna, a cake made with oil. Whoever wrote it knew the Greek Bible and was making John the man who lived on wilderness bread. We hold Brenton's English, not the Greek of the Septuagint, so the word itself is checked through the claims file (claims/bible-greek-hebrew.md), not here.

KAM'S "KINGS" REFERENCE

The Greek Bible's 3 Kingdoms 12:24i (Brenton): "And the woman arose, and took in her hand bread, and two cakes, and grapes, and a pot of honey, for Achia".

(christianity/Incoming/septuagint-brenton/11-1-kings.md)

A prophet fed with bread, cakes and honey. The Hebrew of the same story (KJV 1 Kings 14:3, beside this) has loaves, cracknels and a cruse of honey.

WHAT ELSE THE GOSPELS SAY ABOUT HIS FOOD

Luke 1:15: he "shall drink neither wine nor strong drink", a Nazirite from birth.

Luke 7:33: he "came neither eating bread nor drinking wine". Matthew 11:18: "neither eating nor drinking".

These describe abstinence, not a menu. They fit a John who did not eat what others ate. They do not settle which wilderness food he did eat.

THE SAME HOUSEHOLD'S TRADITION

Hegesippus says James, the brother of Jesus, was holy from his mother's womb, drank no wine and ate no flesh. A fleshless John in the Ebionite gospel sits beside a fleshless James in Hegesippus: the same picture of holiness. The source card is beside this.

THE CAROB CLAIM

In the debate: "The body of evidence around John's diet is uh carob carropods. The locust bean." (3:13:26)

What holds: carob pods are a real wilderness food, and the gospels name them. The "husks that the swine did eat" in Luke 15:16 are κερατια, carob pods, in the Greek (Westcott-Hort: "εκ των κερατιων"). Carob is still called "locust bean" and "St John's bread" in English.

What doesn't hold yet: no ancient text we hold says John ate carob. The names connect the carob to John; they do not show who first connected them, or when. The earliest source for that is on the list in section 6.

Different from the honey cake: the cake is a reading in an ancient gospel; the carob is an interpretation of the word locust.
The body of evidence around John's diet is uh carob

THE SENTENCE THAT HOLDS EVERY WORD

"Our earliest gospel says John ate locusts. The gospel of the Jewish-Christian movement, quoted by Epiphanius, said honey that tasted of manna, using the Greek Bible's own word for it. So a fleshless John is an old reading, kept by a Jewish-Christian movement, not a modern invention. Which reading came first is contested."

WHICH CAME FIRST? THE HONEST STATE OF IT

FOR LOCUSTS FIRST: Mark is usually dated earliest; every gospel manuscript we know of reads locusts; the Ebionite gospel looks to most scholars like a later Greek text that draws on the canonical ones.

FOR THE CAKE FIRST: Kam's argument, after Edwards, is that the Hebrew gospel came first and the canonical Greek gospels drew on it. On that view the manna reading could be the older one and "locusts" the change.

That is a question about the whole Hebrew gospel, not this one verse. The verse cannot settle it by itself.

WHERE OUR SIDE OVERREACHES

"We definitely know it wasn't locust bugs." No text we hold supports "definitely".

"A honey-cake tradition in the church fathers." The fathers we hold say locusts; the cake is one gospel, quoted once.

"Carob." A later interpretation, not an ancient reading, until someone finds the source.

WHERE THE OTHER SIDE OVERREACHES

"Epiphanius proves they changed it." He assumes it. He writes as their opponent, and the pun shows only that the two readings met in Greek.

"Locusts make John a meat-eater." Epiphanius himself says John ate no meat and still ate locusts (30,19,3). And the Damascus Document gives locusts a rule of their own, next to the rule for fish.

WHAT WE WOULD LIKE TO GET HOLD OF

1. THE DAMASCUS DOCUMENT in a named public-domain translation (Schechter 1910), so the locust rule can be held, not just pointed at.

2. A CRITICAL APPARATUS for Matthew 3:4 and Mark 1:6, to state exactly what the manuscripts read.

3. THE FIRST SOURCE THAT TIES CAROB TO JOHN, with its date.

4. ISIDORE OF PELUSIUM, reported to have read John's akrides as the tips of plants rather than insects. Unchecked: we have not seen the text.

5. THE SLAVONIC JOSEPHUS on John, which OPEN-RESEARCH.md item 3 says describes a Baptist who ate no flesh. A late and disputed text; worth holding so it can be described exactly.

6. JAMES EDWARDS, The Hebrew Gospel (2009), the scholarship behind Kam's side. In copyright: notes and short quotes only.

WHERE THIS GOES NEXT

OPEN-RESEARCH.md item 3 asks for exactly this: a section on the sacrifice case file, under Questions People Raise, giving the objection, the variant stated exactly, and the honest limit. This board is the material for it. The case file itself changes only after someone has checked the sources.
